paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James took place in Madison, Florida, in February 1881, after the two Black men were arrested for shooting Frank P. Patterson, a young lawyer, in the Madison court house on February 8 during testimony in a contested congressional election. Whites threatened to lynch the prisoners while Black residents armed to protect them, and militia guarded the jail until the men were moved to Tallahassee. The papers treated the affair as a partisan matter, and in August 1882 the two men, by then convicted and granted a new trial, were shot dead by a mob at Madison.

Testimony in the contest between Republican Horatio Bisbee Jr. and Democrat J. J. Finley was being taken before Dennis Eagan, the federal internal revenue collector, acting as a notary public. On February 7 Savage, described as "a noted negro politician," testified for Bisbee and, by a Democratic account, swore that Patterson had handed doubled tickets to Democratic voters. Sheriff S. M. Hankins testified that he held a perjury warrant for Savage that morning.

On February 8, after Patterson read Savage's testimony in the court house, Savage held him with one arm and shot him in the body, and James fired a shot that struck his hand; Patterson died about an hour later. Deputy Sheriff Charles S. Church locked the armed pair in the court room, and when Hankins returned with a posse Savage "said he would surrender if I would protect him from being murdered."

With a mostly Black crowd outside, the Savannah Morning News correspondent wrote, "the whites threatening to lynch the prisoners, and the negroes declaring they should be protected." The first Tallahassee wire said Savage was "threatened with lynch law" and that both races were arming, while the Weekly Floridian spoke of "some talk of lynching" among whites and threats of rescue by Black residents. A Washington account added that a Black crowd at the jail threatened to free the prisoners until Judge Vann addressed them.

The Governor's Guards and a Monticello company reached Madison by special train that night and stacked arms in front of the jail. Their commander, Captain Mosely, reported armed Black squads but said "No armed whites were visible, except the military." Eagan, wanted as an accessory, was guarded at his house by armed Black men, then fled and was arrested at Albany, Georgia.
Relief companies from Jacksonville and Lake City took over the guard, and on February 16 the Jacksonville Light Infantry moved the prisoners to Tallahassee "very quietly."

Savage and James were tried for murder at Jasper in June 1881 before a jury of eleven whites and one Black man. Witnesses said the dying Patterson named both men, while a defense witness, Jethro Robinson, said Patterson struck first and was impeached in rebuttal. During the trial one Madison witness, C. P. Coyle, mortally wounded another, Joel A. Phillips.

No verdict appears in the June coverage, but an 1882 dispatch said the men had been convicted and granted a new trial. On August 25, 1882, as they were taken by train from Tallahassee to Jasper, about one hundred people met the train at Madison and twelve or fifteen boarded it and shot both prisoners; the wires had been cut.

Most coverage came from Democratic papers that framed the killing as a political murder by a Black Republican. The Weekly Floridian called Savage "a violent and unprincipled negro politician," and the Wilmington Daily Gazette headlined "Grist for the Outrage Mill" and called him "a negro bully." The Savannah Morning News reported the lynch threats plainly but stressed that Republicans were making political capital of the case.

Republican papers first told another story: the Portland Daily Press ran Jenkins' telegram that Savage had been attacked under "Florida Democrats Intimidating His Witnesses," and the Chicago Tribune labeled the Madison dispatch the "Bulldozers' Account." In 1882 the Jacksonville wire on the train killing ran as "Two Florida Murderers Killed," without condemning the mob.

The Savannah correspondent and Robinson said Patterson struck Savage first, while Deputy Church testified that no blows were exchanged. Eagan was variously said to have cried "Kill him," "shoot him" or "Give him another shot," which he denied.

bases: Whites threatened to lynch the two Black prisoners held for the killing of Patterson and troops were sent to guard the jail (A1, A4, A9); no attack on them occurred in 1881, so the stage is threatened.

The Savannah wire and letters (A1, A2, A4) and the Tallahassee Weekly Floridian (A9) each report white lynch threats against the prisoners and the troops sent to guard them; the Wilmington Gazette and Chicago and Sacramento dispatches confirm the shooting, arrest and jail guard (A5, A6, A14).

accounts.label: Deputy Sheriff Church (trial)

accounts.label: Dennis Eagan (statement and trial)
accounts.gist: He saw a scuffle, then shooting by Savage, made no remark, and urged Savage to surrender; Savage's forehead was bleeding and Savage said Patterson had hit him.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called it a 'deplorable tragedy', reported the white lynch threats plainly, and blamed Republicans for making 'capital' of it.

The Weekly Floridian condemned Savage as a 'violent and unprincipled negro politician' and the killing as 'cold-blooded', while describing the white lynch talk as 'intemperate action' prevented by the militia.
The Wilmington Daily Gazette headlined 'Grist for the Outrage Mill' and called Savage 'a negro bully' and a 'Republican murderer'.
The Portland Daily Press headlined 'Florida Democrats Intimidating His Witnesses', and the Chicago Tribune ran the Madison dispatch as the 'Bulldozers' Account'.
In 1882 the Jacksonville wire called the prisoners 'Two Florida Murderers' who 'Meet their Doom'.
